00015| Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. You use React Components to build user interfaces, and Next.js for additional features and optimizations.

00013| ## Proxy
00014| 
00015| > **Good to know**: Starting with Next.js 16, Middleware is now called Proxy to better reflect its purpose. The functionality remains the same.
00016| 
00017| Proxy allows you to run code before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.
00018| 
00019| ### Use cases
00020| 
00021| Some common scenarios where Proxy is effective include:
00022| 
00023| - Modifying headers for all pages or a subset of pages
00024| - Rewriting to different pages based on A/B tests or experiments
00025| - Programmatic redirects based on incoming request properties
00026| 
00027| For simple redirects, consider using the [`redirects`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/redirects) configuration in `next.config.ts` first. Proxy should be used when you need access to request data or more complex logic.
00028| 
00029| Proxy is _not_ intended for slow data fetching. While Proxy can be helpful for [optimistic checks](/docs/app/guides/authentication#optimistic-checks-with-proxy-optional) such as permission-based redirects, it should not be used as a full session management or authorization solution.
00030| 
00031| Using fetch with `options.cache`, `options.next.revalidate`, or `options.next.tags`, has no effect in Proxy.
00032| 
00033| ### Convention
00034| 
00035| Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.
00036| 
00037| > **Note**: While only one `proxy.ts` file is supported per project, you can still organize your proxy logic into modules. Break out proxy functionalities into separate `.ts` or `.js` files and import them into your main `proxy.ts` file. This allows for cleaner management of route-specific proxy, aggregated in the `proxy.ts` for centralized control. By enforcing a single proxy file, it simplifies configuration, prevents potential conflicts, and optimizes performance by avoiding multiple proxy layers.
00038| 
00039| ### Example
00040| 
00041| You can export your proxy function as either a default export or a named `proxy` export:
00042| 
00043| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00044| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00045| import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00046| 
00047| // This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
00048| export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
00049|   return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
00050| }
00051| 
00052| // Alternatively, you can use a default export:
00053| // export default function proxy(request: NextRequest) { ... }
00054| 
00055| export const config = {
00056|   matcher: '/about/:path*',
00057| }
00058| ```
00059| 
00060| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00061| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00062| 
00063| // This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
00064| export function proxy(request) {
00065|   return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
00066| }
00067| 
00068| // Alternatively, you can use a default export:
00069| // export default function proxy(request) { ... }
00070| 
00071| export const config = {
00072|   matcher: '/about/:path*',
00073| }
00074| ```
00075| 
00076| The `matcher` config allows you to filter Proxy to run on specific paths. See the [Matcher](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#matcher) documentation for more details on path matching.
00077| 
00078| Read more about [using `proxy`](/docs/app/guides/backend-for-frontend#proxy), or refer to the `proxy` [API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy).

<file>
00001| ---
00002| title: proxy.js
00003| description: API reference for the proxy.js file.
00004| related:
00005|   title: Learn more about Proxy
00006|   links:
00007|     - app/api-reference/functions/next-request
00008|     - app/api-reference/functions/next-response
00009| ---
00010| 
00011| > **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.
00012| 
00013| The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.
00014| 
00015| Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.
00016| 
00017| > **Good to know**:
00018| >
00019| > Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
00020| >
00021| > To pass information from Proxy to your application, use [headers](#setting-headers), [cookies](#using-cookies), [rewrites](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#rewrite), [redirects](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#redirect), or the URL.
00022| 
00023| Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.
00024| 
00025| If you’ve customized [`pageExtensions`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions), for example to `.page.ts` or `.page.js`, name your file `proxy.page.ts` or `proxy.page.js` accordingly.
00026| 
00027| ```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00028| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00029| import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00030| 
00031| // This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
00032| export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
00033|   return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
00034| }
00035| 
00036| export const config = {
00037|   matcher: '/about/:path*',
00038| }
00039| ```
00040| 
00041| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00042| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00043| 
00044| // This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
00045| export function proxy(request) {
00046|   return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
00047| }
00048| 
00049| export const config = {
00050|   matcher: '/about/:path*',
00051| }
00052| ```
00053| 
00054| ## Exports
00055| 
00056| ### Proxy function
00057| 
00058| The file must export a single function, either as a default export or named `proxy`. Note that multiple proxy from the same file are not supported.
00059| 
00060| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00061| // Example of default export
00062| export default function proxy(request) {
00063|   // Proxy logic
00064| }
00065| ```
00066| 
00067| ### Config object (optional)
00068| 
00069| Optionally, a config object can be exported alongside the Proxy function. This object includes the [matcher](#matcher) to specify paths where the Proxy applies.
00070| 
00071| ### Matcher
00072| 
00073| The `matcher` option allows you to target specific paths for the Proxy to run on.
00074| 
00075| Without a `matcher`, Proxy runs on **every request**, including static files (`_next/static`), image optimizations (`_next/image`), and assets in the `public/` folder. Consider using a [negative match pattern](#negative-matching) to exclude these paths, otherwise auth logic or redirects can unintentionally block CSS, JS, or images from loading.
00076| 
00077| You can specify paths in several ways:
00078| 
00079| - For a single path: Directly use a string to define the path, like `'/about'`.
00080| - For multiple paths: Use an array to list multiple paths, such as `matcher: ['/about', '/contact']`, which applies the Proxy to both `/about` and `/contact`.
00081| 
00082| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00083| export const config = {
00084|   matcher: ['/about/:path*', '/dashboard/:path*'],
00085| }
00086| ```
00087| 
00088| Additionally, the `matcher` option supports complex path specifications using regular expressions. For example, you can exclude certain paths with a regular expression matcher:
00089| 
00090| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00091| export const config = {
00092|   matcher: [
00093|     // Exclude API routes, static files, image optimizations, and .png files
00094|     '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|.*\\.png$).*)',
00095|   ],
00096| }
00097| ```
00098| 
00099| This enables precise control over which paths to include or exclude.
00100| 
00101| The `matcher` option accepts an array of objects with the following keys:
00102| 
00103| - `source`: The path or pattern used to match the request paths. It can be a string for direct path matching or a pattern for more complex matching.
00104| - `locale` (optional): A boolean that, when set to `false`, ignores locale-based routing in path matching.
00105| - `has` (optional): Specifies conditions based on the presence of specific request elements such as headers, query parameters, or cookies.
00106| - `missing` (optional): Focuses on conditions where certain request elements are absent, like missing headers or cookies.
00107| 
00108| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00109| export const config = {
00110|   matcher: [
00111|     {
00112|       source: '/api/:path*',
00113|       locale: false,
00114|       has: [
00115|         { type: 'header', key: 'Authorization', value: 'Bearer Token' },
00116|         { type: 'query', key: 'userId', value: '123' },
00117|       ],
00118|       missing: [{ type: 'cookie', key: 'session', value: 'active' }],
00119|     },
00120|   ],
00121| }
00122| ```
00123| 
00124| The `source` path patterns:
00125| 
00126| 1. MUST start with `/`
00127| 2. Can include named parameters: `/about/:path` matches `/about/a` and `/about/b` but not `/about/a/c`
00128| 3. Can have modifiers on named parameters (starting with `:`): `/about/:path*` matches `/about/a/b/c` because `*` is _zero or more_. `?` is _zero or one_ and `+` _one or more_
00129| 4. Can use regular expression enclosed in parenthesis: `/about/(.*)` is the same as `/about/:path*`
00130| 5. Are anchored to the start of the path: `/about` matches `/about` and `/about/team` but not `/blog/about`
00131| 
00132| Read more details on [path-to-regexp](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp#path-to-regexp-1) documentation.
00133| 
00134| > **Good to know**:
00135| >
00136| > - The `matcher` values need to be constants so they can be statically analyzed at build-time. Dynamic values such as variables will be ignored.
00137| > - For backward compatibility, Next.js always considers `/public` as `/public/index`. Therefore, a matcher of `/public/:path` will match.
00138| 
00139| ## Params
00140| 
00141| ### `request`
00142| 
00143| When defining Proxy, the default export function accepts a single parameter, `request`. This parameter is an instance of `NextRequest`, which represents the incoming HTTP request.
00144| 
00145| ```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00146| import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00147| 
00148| export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
00149|   // Proxy logic goes here
00150| }
00151| ```
00152| 
00153| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00154| export function proxy(request) {
00155|   // Proxy logic goes here
00156| }
00157| ```
00158| 
00159| If you prefer a shorthand, you can use the `NextProxy` type. It infers the parameter types for both `request` (`NextRequest`) and `event` (`NextFetchEvent`) automatically:
00160| 
00161| ```tsx filename="proxy.ts"
00162| import type { NextProxy } from 'next/server'
00163| 
00164| export const proxy: NextProxy = (request, event) => {
00165|   event.waitUntil(Promise.resolve())
00166|   return Response.json({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname })
00167| }
00168| ```
00169| 
00170| > **Good to know**:
00171| >
00172| > - `NextRequest` is a type that represents incoming HTTP requests in Next.js Proxy, whereas [`NextResponse`](#nextresponse) is a class used to manipulate and send back HTTP responses.
00173| 
00174| ## NextResponse
00175| 
00176| The `NextResponse` API allows you to:
00177| 
00178| - `redirect` the incoming request to a different URL
00179| - `rewrite` the response by displaying a given URL
00180| - Set request headers for API Routes, `getServerSideProps`, and `rewrite` destinations
00181| - Set response cookies
00182| - Set response headers
00183| 
00184| <AppOnly>
00185| 
00186| To produce a response from Proxy, you can:
00187| 
00188| 1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route)) that produces a response
00189| 2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)
00190| 
00191| > **Good to know**: For redirects, you can also use `Response.redirect` instead of `NextResponse.redirect`.
00192| 
00193| </AppOnly>
00194| 
00195| <PagesOnly>
00196| 
00197| To produce a response from Proxy, you can:
00198| 
00199| 1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/pages-and-layouts) or [Edge API Route](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/api-routes)) that produces a response
00200| 2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)
00201| 
00202| </PagesOnly>
00203| 
00204| ## Execution order
00205| 
00206| Proxy will be invoked for **every route in your project**. Given this, it's crucial to use [matchers](#matcher) to precisely target or exclude specific routes. The following is the execution order:
00207| 
00208| 1. `headers` from `next.config.js`
00209| 2. `redirects` from `next.config.js`
00210| 3. Proxy (`rewrites`, `redirects`, etc.)
00211| 4. `beforeFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
00212| 5. Filesystem routes (`public/`, `_next/static/`, `pages/`, `app/`, etc.)
00213| 6. `afterFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
00214| 7. Dynamic Routes (`/blog/[slug]`)
00215| 8. `fallback` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
00216| 
00217| > **Good to know:** [Server Functions](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-server) are not separate routes in this chain. They are handled as POST requests to the route where they are used, so a Proxy matcher that excludes a path will also skip Server Function calls on that path.
00218| >
00219| > A matcher change or a refactor that moves a Server Function to a different route can silently remove Proxy coverage. Always verify authentication and authorization inside each Server Function rather than relying on Proxy alone. See the [Data Security guide](/docs/app/guides/data-security#authentication-and-authorization) for recommended patterns.
00220| 
00221| ## Runtime
00222| 
00223| Proxy defaults to using the Node.js runtime. The [`runtime`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/runtime) config option is not available in Proxy files. Setting the `runtime` config option in Proxy will throw an error.
00224| 
00225| ## Advanced Proxy flags
00226| 
00227| In `v13.1` of Next.js two additional flags were introduced for proxy, `skipProxyUrlNormalize` (formerly `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize`) and `skipTrailingSlashRedirect` to handle advanced use cases.
00228| 
00229| `skipTrailingSlashRedirect` disables Next.js redirects for adding or removing trailing slashes. This allows custom handling inside proxy to maintain the trailing slash for some paths but not others, which can make incremental migrations easier.
00230| 
00231| ```js filename="next.config.js"
00232| module.exports = {
00233|   skipTrailingSlashRedirect: true,
00234| }
00235| ```
00236| 
00237| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00238| const legacyPrefixes = ['/docs', '/blog']
00239| 
00240| export default async function proxy(req) {
00241|   const { pathname } = req.nextUrl
00242| 
00243|   if (legacyPrefixes.some((prefix) => pathname.startsWith(prefix))) {
00244|     return NextResponse.next()
00245|   }
00246| 
00247|   // apply trailing slash handling
00248|   if (
00249|     !pathname.endsWith('/') &&
00250|     !pathname.match(/((?!\.well-known(?:\/.*)?)(?:[^/]+\/)*[^/]+\.\w+)/)
00251|   ) {
00252|     return NextResponse.redirect(
00253|       new URL(`${req.nextUrl.pathname}/`, req.nextUrl)
00254|     )
00255|   }
00256| }
00257| ```
00258| 
00259| `skipProxyUrlNormalize` allows for disabling the URL normalization in Next.js to make handling direct visits and client-transitions the same. In some advanced cases, this option provides full control by using the original URL.
00260| 
00261| ```js filename="next.config.js"
00262| module.exports = {
00263|   skipProxyUrlNormalize: true,
00264| }
00265| ```
00266| 
00267| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00268| export default async function proxy(req) {
00269|   const { pathname } = req.nextUrl
00270| 
00271|   // GET /_next/data/build-id/hello.json
00272| 
00273|   console.log(pathname)
00274|   // with the flag this now /_next/data/build-id/hello.json
00275|   // without the flag this would be normalized to /hello
00276| }
00277| ```
00278| 
00279| ## Examples
00280| 
00281| ### Conditional Statements
00282| 
00283| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00284| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00285| import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00286|

00312| ### Using Cookies

00314| Cookies are regular headers. On a `Request`, they are stored in the `Cookie` header. On a `Response` they are in the `Set-Cookie` header. Next.js provides a convenient way to access and manipulate these cookies through the `cookies` extension on `NextRequest` and `NextResponse`.
00315| 
00316| 1. For incoming requests, `cookies` comes with the following methods: `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete` cookies. You can check for the existence of a cookie with `has` or remove all cookies with `clear`.
00317| 2. For outgoing responses, `cookies` have the following methods `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete`.

00384| You can set request and response headers using the `NextResponse` API (setting _request_ headers is available since Next.js v13.0.0).

00396|   const response = NextResponse.next({

00399|       headers: requestHeaders,
00400|     },
00401|   })
00402|

00404|   response.headers.set('x-hello-from-proxy2', 'hello')

00440| #### RSC requests and rewrites
00441| 
00442| During RSC requests, Next.js strips internal Flight headers from the `request` instance in Proxy. 00602| ### Negative matching
00603| 
00604| The `matcher` config allows full regex so matching like negative lookaheads or character matching is supported. An example of a negative lookahead to match all except specific paths can be seen here:

00606| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00607| export const config = {
00608|   matcher: [

00610|      * Match all request paths except for the ones starting with:
00611|      * - api (API routes)
00612|      * - _next/static (static files)
00613|      * - _next/image (image optimization files)
00614|      * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
00615|      */
00616|     '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
00617|   ],

00631|      * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
00632|      */

00647|         { type: 'header', key: 'purpose', value: 'prefetch' },
00648|       ],

00674| ### `waitUntil` and `NextFetchEvent`
00675| 
00676| The `NextFetchEvent` object extends the native [`FetchEvent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/FetchEvent) object, and includes the [`waitUntil()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/ExtendableEvent/waitUntil) method.

00678| The `waitUntil()` method takes a promise as an argument, and extends the lifetime of the Proxy until the promise settles. This is useful for performing work in the background.
00679| 
00680| ```ts filename="proxy.ts"
00681| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00682| import type { NextFetchEvent, NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00683| 
00684| export function proxy(req: NextRequest, event: NextFetchEvent) {
00685|   event.waitUntil(

00687|       method: 'POST',
00688|       body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: req.nextUrl.pathname }),
00689|     })
00690|   )
00691| 
00692|   return NextResponse.next()
00693| }
00694| ```

00696| ### Unit testing (experimental)
00697| 
00698| Starting in Next.js 15.1, the `next/experimental/testing/server` package contains utilities to help unit test proxy files. Unit testing proxy can help ensure that it's only run on desired paths and that custom routing logic works as intended before code reaches production.

00700| The `unstable_doesProxyMatch` function can be used to assert whether proxy will run for the provided URL, headers, and cookies.
00701| 
00702| ```js
00703| import { unstable_doesProxyMatch } from 'next/experimental/testing/server'
00704| 
00705| expect(
00706|   unstable_doesProxyMatch({
00707|     config,
00708|     nextConfig,
00709|     url: '/test',
00710|   })
00711| ).toEqual(false)
00712| ```

00714| The entire proxy function can also be tested.

00716| ```js

00718| 
00719| const request = new NextRequest('https://nextjs.org/docs')

00736| 
00737| ## Migration to Proxy
00738| 
00739| ### Why the Change
00740| 
00741| The reason behind the renaming of `middleware` is that the term "middleware" can often be confused with Express.js middleware, leading to a misinterpretation of its purpose. Also, Middleware is highly capable, so it may encourage the usage; however, this feature is recommended to be used as a last resort.
00742| 
00743| Next.js is moving forward to provide better APIs with better ergonomics so that developers can achieve their goals without Middleware. This is the reason behind the renaming of `middleware`.
00744| 
00745| ### Why "Proxy"
00746| 
00747| The name Proxy clarifies what Middleware is capable of. The term "proxy" implies a network boundary in front of the app, which is how this feature behaves. It can run outside of your application’s main runtime and handle requests before they reach your app. These characteristics align better with the term "proxy" and provide a clearer purpose for the feature.
00748| 
00749| ### How to Migrate
00750| 
00751| We recommend users avoid relying on Middleware unless no other options exist. Our goal is to give them APIs with better ergonomics so they can achieve their goals without Middleware.
00752| 
00753| The term “middleware” often confuses users with Express.js middleware, which can encourage misuse. To clarify our direction, we are renaming the file convention to “proxy.” This highlights that we are moving away from Middleware, breaking down its overloaded features, and making the Proxy clear in its purpose.
00754| 
00755| Next.js provides a codemod to migrate from `middleware.ts` to `proxy.ts`. You can run the following command to migrate:
00756| 
00757| ```bash
00758| npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy .
00759| ```
00760| 
00761| The codemod will rename the file and the function name from `middleware` to `proxy`.
00762| 
00763| ```diff
00764| // middleware.ts -> proxy.ts
00765| 
00766| - export function middleware() {
00767| + export function proxy() {
00768| ```

> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.

The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.

Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.

> **Good to know**:
>
> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.

00054| ## Exports
00055| 
00056| ### Proxy function
00057| 
00058| The file must export a single function, either as a default export or named `proxy`. Note that multiple proxy from the same file are not supported.
00059| 
00060| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00061| // Example of default export
00062| export default function proxy(request) {
00063|   // Proxy logic
00064| }
00065| ```
00066| 
00067| ### Config object (optional)
00068| 
00069| Optionally, a config object can be exported alongside the Proxy function. This object includes the [matcher](#matcher) to specify paths where the Proxy applies.
00070| 
00071| ### Matcher
00072| 
00073| The `matcher` option allows you to target specific paths for the Proxy to run on.
00074| 
00075| Without a `matcher`, Proxy runs on **every request**, including static files (`_next/static`), image optimizations (`_next/image`), and assets in the `public/` folder. Consider using a [negative match pattern](#negative-matching) to exclude these paths, otherwise auth logic or redirects can unintentionally block CSS, JS, or images from loading.
00076| 
00077| You can specify paths in several ways:
00078| 
00079| - For a single path: Directly use a string to define the path, like `'/about'`.
00080| - For multiple paths: Use an array to list multiple paths, such as `matcher: ['/about', '/contact']`, which applies the Proxy to both `/about` and `/contact`.
00081| 
00082| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00083| export const config = {
00084|   matcher: ['/about/:path*', '/dashboard/:path*'],
00085| }
00086| ```
00087| 
00088| Additionally, the `matcher` option supports complex path specifications using regular expressions. For example, you can exclude certain paths with a regular expression matcher:
00089| 
00090| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00091| export const config = {
00092|   matcher: [
00093|     // Exclude API routes, static files, image optimizations, and .png files
00094|     '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|.*\\.png$).*)',
00095|   ],
00096| }
00097| ```
00098| 
00099| This enables precise control over which paths to include or exclude.
00100| 
00101| The `matcher` option accepts an array of objects with the following keys:
00102| 
00103| - `source`: The path or pattern used to match the request paths. It can be a string for direct path matching or a pattern for more complex matching.
00104| - `locale` (optional): A boolean that, when set to `false`, ignores locale-based routing in path matching.
00105| - `has` (optional): Specifies conditions based on the presence of specific request elements such as headers, query parameters, or cookies.
00106| - `missing` (optional): Focuses on conditions where certain request elements are absent, like missing headers or cookies.
00107| 
00108| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00109| export const config = {
00110|   matcher: [
00111|     {
00112|       source: '/api/:path*',
00113|       locale: false,
00114|       has: [
00115|         { type: 'header', key: 'Authorization', value: 'Bearer Token' },
00116|         { type: 'query', key: 'userId', value: '123' },
00117|       ],
00118|       missing: [{ type: 'cookie', key: 'session', value: 'active' }],
00119|     },
00120|   ],
00121| }
00122| ```
00123| 
00124| The `source` path patterns:
00125| 
00126| 1. MUST start with `/`
00127| 2. Can include named parameters: `/about/:path` matches `/about/a` and `/about/b` but not `/about/a/c`
00128| 3. Can have modifiers on named parameters (starting with `:`): `/about/:path*` matches `/about/a/b/c` because `*` is _zero or more_. `?` is _zero or one_ and `+` _one or more_
00129| 4. Can use regular expression enclosed in parenthesis: `/about/(.*)` is the same as `/about/:path*`
00130| 5. Are anchored to the start of the path: `/about` matches `/about` and `/about/team` but not `/blog/about`
00131| 
00132| Read more details on [path-to-regexp](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp#path-to-regexp-1) documentation.
00133| 
00134| > **Good to know**:
00135| >
00136| > - The `matcher` values need to be constants so they can be statically analyzed at build-time. Dynamic values such as variables will be ignored.
00137| > - For backward compatibility, Next.js always considers `/public` as `/public/index`. Therefore, a matcher of `/public/:path` will match.

00141| ### `request`
00142| 
00143| When defining Proxy, the default export function accepts a single parameter, `request`. This parameter is an instance of `NextRequest`, which represents the incoming HTTP request.
00144| 
00145| ```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00146| import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00147| 
00148| export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
00149|   // Proxy logic goes here
00150| }

00174| ## NextResponse
00175| 
00176| The `NextResponse` API allows you to:
00177| 
00178| - `redirect` the incoming request to a different URL
00179| - `rewrite` the response by displaying a given URL
00180| - Set request headers for API Routes, `getServerSideProps`, and `rewrite` destinations
00181| - Set response cookies
00182| - Set response headers
00183|

00185|

00187| 
00188| 1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route)) that produces a response
00189| 2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)

00204| ## Execution order
00205| 
00206| Proxy will be invoked for **every route in your project**. Given this, it's crucial to use [matchers](#matcher) to precisely target or exclude specific routes. The following is the execution order:
00207| 
00208| 1. `headers` from `next.config.js`
00209| 2. `redirects` from `next.config.js`
00210| 3. Proxy (`rewrites`, `redirects`, etc.)
00211| 4. `beforeFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
00212| 5. Filesystem routes (`public/`, `_next/static/`, `pages/`, `app/`, etc.)
00213| 6. `afterFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
00214| 7. Dynamic Routes (`/blog/[slug]`)
00215| 8. `fallback` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
00216| 
00217| > **Good to know:** [Server Functions](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-server) are not separate routes in this chain. They are handled as POST requests to the route where they are used, so a Proxy matcher that excludes a path will also skip Server Function calls on that path.
00218| >
00219| > A matcher change or a refactor that moves a Server Function to a different route can silently remove Proxy coverage. Always verify authentication and authorization inside each Server Function rather than relying on Proxy alone. See the [Data Security guide](/docs/app/guides/data-security#authentication-and-authorization) for recommended patterns.
00220| 
00221| ## Runtime
00222| 
00223| Proxy defaults to using the Node.js runtime. The [`runtime`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/runtime) config option is not available in Proxy files. Setting the `runtime` config option in Proxy will throw an error.

00225| ## Advanced Proxy flags
00226| 
00227| In `v13.1` of Next.js two additional flags were introduced for proxy, `skipProxyUrlNormalize` (formerly `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize`) and `skipTrailingSlashRedirect` to handle advanced use cases.
00228| 
00229| `skipTrailingSlashRedirect` disables Next.js redirects for adding or removing trailing slashes. This allows custom handling inside proxy to maintain the trailing slash for some paths but not others, which can make incremental migrations easier.
00230| 
00231| ```js filename="next.config.js"
00232| module.exports = {
00233|   skipTrailingSlashRedirect: true,
00234| }
00235| ```
00236| 
00237| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00238| const legacyPrefixes = ['/docs', '/blog']
00239| 
00240| export default async function proxy(req) {
00241|   const { pathname } = req.nextUrl
00242| 
00243|   if (legacyPrefixes.some((prefix) => pathname.startsWith(prefix))) {
00244|     return NextResponse.next()
00245|   }
00246| 
00247|   // apply trailing slash handling
00248|   if (
00249|     !pathname.endsWith('/') &&
00250|     !pathname.match(/((?!\.well-known(?:\/.*)?)(?:[^/]+\/)*[^/]+\.\w+)/)
00251|   ) {
00252|     return NextResponse.redirect(
00253|       new URL(`${req.nextUrl.pathname}/`, req.nextUrl)
00254|     )
00255|   }
00256| }
00257| ```
00258| 
00259| `skipProxyUrlNormalize` allows for disabling the URL normalization in Next.js to make handling direct visits and client-transitions the same. In some advanced cases, this option provides full control by using the original URL.
00260| 
00261| ```js filename="next.config.js"
00262| module.exports = {
00263|   skipProxyUrlNormalize: true,
00264| }
00265| ```
00266| 
00267| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00268| export default async function proxy(req) {
00269|   const { pathname } = req.nextUrl
00270| 
00271|   // GET /_next/data/build-id/hello.json
00272| 
00273|   console.log(pathname)
00274|   // with the flag this now /_next/data/build-id/hello.json
00275|   // without the flag this would be normalized to /hello
00276| }
00277| ```

00312| ### Using Cookies
00313| 
00314| Cookies are regular headers. On a `Request`, they are stored in the `Cookie` header. On a `Response` they are in the `Set-Cookie` header. Next.js provides a convenient way to access and manipulate these cookies through the `cookies` extension on `NextRequest` and `NextResponse`.
00315| 
00316| 1. For incoming requests, `cookies` comes with the following methods: `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete` cookies. You can check for the existence of a cookie with `has` or remove all cookies with `clear`.
00317| 2. For outgoing responses, `cookies` have the following methods `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete`.
00318| 
00319| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00320| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00321| import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00322| 
00323| export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
00324|   // Assume a "Cookie:nextjs=fast" header to be present on the incoming request
00325|   // Getting cookies from the request using the `RequestCookies` API
00326|   let cookie = request.cookies.get('nextjs')
00327|   console.log(cookie) // => { name: 'nextjs', value: 'fast', Path: '/' }
00328|   const allCookies = request.cookies.getAll()
00329|   console.log(allCookies) // => [{ name: 'nextjs', value: 'fast' }]
00330| 
00331|   request.cookies.has('nextjs') // => true
00332|   request.cookies.delete('nextjs')
00333|   request.cookies.has('nextjs') // => false
00334| 
00335|   // Setting cookies on the response using the `ResponseCookies` API
00336|   const response = NextResponse.next()
00337|   response.cookies.set('vercel', 'fast')
00338|   response.cookies.set({
00339|     name: 'vercel',
00340|     value: 'fast',
00341|     path: '/',
00342|   })
00343|   cookie = response.cookies.get('vercel')
00344|   console.log(cookie) // => { name: 'vercel', value: 'fast', Path: '/' }
00345|   // The outgoing response will have a `Set-Cookie:vercel=fast;path=/` header.
00346| 
00347|   return response
00348| }
00349| ```

00440| #### RSC requests and rewrites
00441| 
00442| During RSC requests, Next.js strips internal Flight headers from the `request` instance in Proxy. For example, headers like `rsc`, `next-router-state-tree`, and `next-router-prefetch` are not exposed through `request.headers`. This is to prevent accidentally handling an RSC request differently than the HTML request as both need to align.
00443| 
00444| When you use `NextResponse.rewrite()`, Next.js automatically propagates the required RSC rewrite headers upstream.
00445| 
00446| If you implement custom rewrite logic with `fetch()` instead of `NextResponse.rewrite()`, you can run into missing RSC headers unless you forward them manually.
00447| 
00448| For custom `fetch` rewrite setups, you can also enable `skipProxyUrlNormalize` in `next.config.js` so your rewrite logic can receive the necessary URL shape and RSC headers from the provided request object:
00449| 
00450| ```js filename="next.config.js"
00451| module.exports = {
00452|   skipProxyUrlNormalize: true,
00453| }
00454| ```

00473|   const origin = request.headers.get('origin') ?? ''

00492|   }

00495|     response.headers.set(key, value)
00496|   })
00497| 
00498|   return response
00499| }

00502|   matcher: '/api/:path*',
00503| }

00739| ### Why the Change

00741| The reason behind the renaming of `middleware` is that the term "middleware" can often be confused with Express.js middleware, leading to a misinterpretation of its purpose. 00745| ### Why "Proxy"

00382| ### Setting Headers

00384| You can set request and response headers using the `NextResponse` API (setting _request_ headers is available since Next.js v13.0.0).

00395|   // You can also set request headers in NextResponse.next
00396|   const response = NextResponse.next({

00399|       headers: requestHeaders,
00400|     },
00401|   })
00402| 
00403|   // Set a new response header `x-hello-from-proxy2`
00404|   response.headers.set('x-hello-from-proxy2', 'hello')

00440| #### RSC requests and rewrites
00441| 
00442| During RSC requests, Next.js strips internal Flight headers from the `request` instance in Proxy. For example, headers like `rsc`, `next-router-state-tree`, and `next-router-prefetch` are not exposed through `request.headers`. 00443| 
00444| When you use `NextResponse.rewrite()`, Next.js automatically propagates the required RSC rewrite headers upstream.

00446| If you implement custom rewrite logic with `fetch()` instead of `NextResponse.rewrite()`, you can run into missing RSC headers unless you forward them manually.

00448| For custom `fetch` rewrite setups, you can also enable `skipProxyUrlNormalize` in `next.config.js` so your rewrite logic can receive the necessary URL shape and RSC headers from the provided request object:

00452|   skipProxyUrlNormalize: true,
00453| }
00454| ```

00458| You can set CORS headers in Proxy to allow cross-origin requests, including [simple](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#simple_requests) and [preflighted](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#preflighted_requests) requests.

00557| ### Producing a response
00558| 
00559| You can respond from Proxy directly by returning a `Response` or `NextResponse` instance. (This is available since [Next.js v13.1.0](https://nextjs.org/blog/next-13-1#nextjs-advanced-proxy))

00602| ### Negative matching
00603| 
00604| The `matcher` config allows full regex so matching like negative lookaheads or character matching is supported. An example of a negative lookahead to match all except specific paths can be seen here:

00606| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00607| export const config = {
00608|   matcher: [

00610|      * Match all request paths except for the ones starting with:
00611|      * - api (API routes)
00612|      * - _next/static (static files)
00613|      * - _next/image (image optimization files)
00614|      * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
00615|      */
00616|     '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
00617|   ],
00618| }
00619| ```

00627|      * Match all request paths except for the ones starting with:

00630|      * - _next/image (image optimization files)
00631|      * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
00632|      */
00633|     {

00635|         '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
00636|       missing: [

00638|         { type: 'header', key: 'purpose', value: 'prefetch' },
00639|       ],
00640|     },
00641|

00643|       source:
00644|         '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
00645|       has: [
00646|         { type: 'header', key: 'next-router-prefetch' },
00647|         { type: 'header', key: 'purpose', value: 'prefetch' },
00648|       ],
00649|     },
00650| 
00651|     {
00652|       source:
00653|         '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
00654|       has: [{ type: 'header', key: 'x-present' }],

00665| ```js filename="proxy.js"

00667|   matcher:
00668|     '/((?!api|_next/data|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
00669| }
00670| 
00671| // Proxy will still run for /_next/data/* routes despite being excluded
00672| ```

00674| ### `waitUntil` and `NextFetchEvent`
00675| 
00676| The `NextFetchEvent` object extends the native [`FetchEvent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/FetchEvent) object, and includes the [`waitUntil()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/ExtendableEvent/waitUntil) method.
00677| 
00678| The `waitUntil()` method takes a promise as an argument, and extends the lifetime of the Proxy until the promise settles. This is useful for performing work in the background.
00679| 
00680| ```ts filename="proxy.ts"
00681| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00682| import type { NextFetchEvent, NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00683| 
00684| export function proxy(req: NextRequest, event: NextFetchEvent) {
00685|   event.waitUntil(
00686|     fetch('https://my-analytics-platform.com', {
00687|       method: 'POST',
00688|       body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: req.nextUrl.pathname }),
00689|     })
00690|   )
00691| 
00692|   return NextResponse.next()
00693| }
00694| ```
00695| 
00696| ### Unit testing (experimental)
00697| 
00698| Starting in Next.js 15.1, the `next/experimental/testing/server` package contains utilities to help unit test proxy files. Unit testing proxy can help ensure that it's only run on desired paths and that custom routing logic works as intended before code reaches production.
00699| 
00700| The `unstable_doesProxyMatch` function can be used to assert whether proxy will run for the provided URL, headers, and cookies.
00701| 
00702| ```js
00703| import { unstable_doesProxyMatch } from 'next/experimental/testing/server'
00704| 
00705| expect(
00706|   unstable_doesProxyMatch({
00707|     config,
00708|     nextConfig,
00709|     url: '/test',
00710|   })
00711| ).toEqual(false)
00712| ```
00713| 
00714| The entire proxy function can also be tested.
00715| 
00716| ```js
00717| import { isRewrite, getRewrittenUrl } from 'next/experimental/testing/server'
00718| 
00719| const request = new NextRequest('https://nextjs.org/docs')
00720| const response = await proxy(request)
00721| expect(isRewrite(response)).toEqual(true)
00722| expect(getRewrittenUrl(response)).toEqual('https://other-domain.com/docs')
00723| // getRedirectUrl could also be used if the response were a redirect
00724| ```

00726| ## Platform support
00727| 
00728| | Deployment Option                                                   | Supported         |
00729| | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
00730| | [Node.js server](/docs/app/getting-started/deploying#nodejs-server) | Yes               |
00731| | [Docker container](/docs/app/getting-started/deploying#docker)      | Yes               |
00732| | [Static export](/docs/app/getting-started/deploying#static-export)  | No                |
00733| | [Adapters](/docs/app/getting-started/deploying#adapters)            | Platform-specific |
00734| 
00735| Learn how to [configure Proxy](/docs/app/guides/self-hosting#proxy) when self-hosting Next.js.
00736| 
00737| ## Migration to Proxy
00738| 
00739| ### Why the Change
00740| 
00741| The reason behind the renaming of `middleware` is that the term "middleware" can often be confused with Express.js middleware, leading to a misinterpretation of its purpose. Also, Middleware is highly capable, so it may encourage the usage; however, this feature is recommended to be used as a last resort.
00742| 
00743| Next.js is moving forward to provide better APIs with better ergonomics so that developers can achieve their goals without Middleware. This is the reason behind the renaming of `middleware`.
00744| 
00745| ### Why "Proxy"
00746| 
00747| The name Proxy clarifies what Middleware is capable of. The term "proxy" implies a network boundary in front of the app, which is how this feature behaves. It can run outside of your application’s main runtime and handle requests before they reach your app. These characteristics align better with the term "proxy" and provide a clearer purpose for the feature.
00748| 
00749| ### How to Migrate
00750| 
00751| We recommend users avoid relying on Middleware unless no other options exist. Our goal is to give them APIs with better ergonomics so they can achieve their goals without Middleware.
00752| 
00753| The term “middleware” often confuses users with Express.js middleware, which can encourage misuse. To clarify our direction, we are renaming the file convention to “proxy.” This highlights that we are moving away from Middleware, breaking down its overloaded features, and making the Proxy clear in its purpose.
00754| 
00755| Next.js provides a codemod to migrate from `middleware.ts` to `proxy.ts`. You can run the following command to migrate:
00756| 
00757| ```bash
00758| npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy .
00759| ```
00760| 
00761| The codemod will rename the file and the function name from `middleware` to `proxy`.
00762| 
00763| ```diff
00764| // middleware.ts -> proxy.ts
00765| 
00766| - export function middleware() {
00767| + export function proxy() {
00768| ```
00769| 
00770| ## Version history
00771| 
00772| | Version   | Changes                                                                                       |
00773| | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
00774| | `v16.0.0` | Middleware is deprecated and renamed to Proxy. Proxy defaults to the Node.js runtime          |
00775| | `v15.5.0` | Middleware can now use the Node.js runtime (stable)                                           |
00776| | `v15.2.0` | Middleware can now use the Node.js runtime (experimental)                                     |
00777| | `v13.1.0` | Advanced Middleware flags added                                                               |
00778| | `v13.0.0` | Middleware can modify request headers, response headers, and send responses                   |

> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.

The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.

Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.

> **Good to know**:
>
> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
